top.line: Remove code: the minimal viable code path
top.para: Code is a liability, and the worst bugs sat in features nobody needed, like Log4j's lookups. Removing code never scaled: it needed maps and tests, and vendors were paid for more. Models now build both. Of 1,500 files in sgit, 428 ran for one use case. Specialists could be paid to keep code small, and users will choose it for speed.

in-short.line: Unused code is risk; models make removal safe
in-short.para: Every line is a capability someone may misuse, and the worst bugs sit in unused features. Removal needed a map and tests; models now provide both. One measured use case kept 428 of 1,500 files and passed. The future is the minimal viable code path, maintained by a fractal market of specialists, and driven by speed, not security.

liability.line: The worst vulnerabilities sat in unneeded features
liability.para: Code is a grant of capability; the mandate is what it was meant to do, and a zero-day is often the gap. Log4Shell came from a 2013 convenience request; ImageTragick, Heartbleed and Text4Shell sat in features most users never touched. Of curl's 239 CVEs, 49 were in protocols most builds could leave out, including both criticals.

why-not.line: Removal needed maps and tests, and paid nothing
why-not.para: To remove code safely you need to know what each piece is for and to prove nothing broke, and most code has neither. Vendors were paid for new features, not for less. The unused-feature figures usually quoted are weaker than they look: Pendo's 80% is its own data, and the Standish figure rests on four applications.

changed.line: Models make the scaffolding and the map cheap
changed.para: Models now write the tests, fixtures and environments that prove a removal is safe, and agents can map what a use case calls. This site kept 428 of 1,500 files for one sgit use case and it passed. Research agrees: debloated PHP apps were 46% smaller and lost up to 60% of CVEs, and most dependency code is never reached.

path.line: Minimal at every level, small enough to check
path.para: A minimal viable company ships minimal products built from minimal features on minimal code paths. Why ship a framework to call three functions? If what is used can be modelled, what is not can go. Small code can be verified, which is how the organisation that ships it can stay accountable when humans no longer review every line.

market.line: Specialists paid to maintain minimal components
market.para: Somebody has to keep small, custom code working, and that is the business: specialists maintaining minimal versions of what they know best, paid for upkeep rather than features. It is fractal, from low-level components to domain glue to user-level apps, and each piece carries its own behaviour, decision and workflow policies, and its Wardley stage.

now.line: AI finds more bugs; less code means fewer
now.para: Published CVEs reached 48,185 in 2025 and 72,812 by September 2026, though Gamblin does not attribute it to AI. Anthropic reported over 500 high-severity finds, DARPA's challenge 18 real ones, and curl has 69 CVEs in 2026, 35 from one AI audit. Android cut memory-safety bugs from 76% to 24% by changing what new code is written in.

driver.line: Users will choose small code for speed
driver.para: Security has never been enough to make people use something. As with sgit, where encryption as a constraint led to better features, minimal code has to win on what users feel: faster, lighter, simpler. A smaller attack surface comes with it. The browser article applies this to the biggest program most of us run.

limits.line: One tool, one use case; the market is proposed
limits.para: The measurement covers one tool and one use case. Removing code can remove what people need, so the map and tests come first. The maintainer market is a proposal. Some figures are vendors' own or vary by method, and the Standish figure is not relied on.

sources.line: A voice memo, research and our own measurement
sources.para: From a voice memo on 18 October 2026 and this site's own measurement of sgit on 14 October. Sources include Apache Log4j, ImageTragick, OpenSSL, OWASP, curl's vulnerability data, USENIX and FSE debloating studies, Endor Labs, Pendo, Tidelift, Jerry Gamblin, Anthropic, DARPA and Google's Android team.
